10059486:
Beckie Drew Veazie LD 1996
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, I am submitting testimony in opposition to LD 1996 on behalf of the Town of Veazie.
General Assistance administrators continue to operate without access to a statewide database, despite the clear operational and oversight benefits such a system would provide. A centralized platform would help prevent duplication, reduce errors, limit opportunities for fraud, and improve the quality of information shared with the Department.
Consistency and fairness in the administration of General Assistance is essential. Municipalities are expected to follow uniform standards, yet we are required to do so without the basic infrastructure needed to share information or track cases across jurisdictions. A statewide database would directly support more efficient and equitable program administration.
The Department has acknowledged in the past that a database would be beneficial. Earlier, a software company presented a proposal for a pilot system that was already under development and priced well below earlier estimates. While this proposal offered a practical path forward, it was ultimately declined, with cost cited as the primary concern.
Without a statewide database, administrators are often required to rely solely on applicant self-reporting, which limits the ability to verify eligibility and prevent duplicate assistance. A centralized system would significantly reduce opportunities for fraud and improve program accountability.
For these reasons, I respectfully urge the committee to vote Ought Not to Pass on LD 1996. Eliminating the statutory requirement for a statewide database would remove an important accountability tool and place additional strain on municipalities, administrators, applicants, and taxpayers across the state.

Maine Mayors Coalition Testimony on LD 1996 An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing
General Assistance
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, the Maine Mayors Coalition is providing testimony in opposition to LD 1996, An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing General Assistance.
The Maine Mayors Coalition is a nonpartisan group representing the mayors of eleven Maine communities - Auburn, Bangor, Biddeford, Lewiston, Portland, Rockland, Saco, Sanford, South Portland, Waterville and Westbrook - and nearly 300,000 residents. The Coalition advocates on behalf of our citizens and municipalities for policies that recognize the vital services Maine cities provide and the positive impact Maine cities have on our state. The Coalition seeks to work in partnership with state and federal elected ofPicials to meet the needs of Maine people.
Our most immediate concerns are providing essential support and housing to people who are in need. As you're well aware, Maine's General Assistance program provides a lifeline for many who Pind themselves in dire Pinancial situations. Over the last several years, more people than ever are relying on the GA program due to the lack of housing supply, costs of homes and rents, and prices for food, clothing, energy and other essentials. We do not expect this need to subside for some time.
Like the state as a whole, our cities have experienced signiPicant increases in GA applicants and costs. For us, these growing numbers place additional burdens on our municipal budgets and staffs as well as on our ability to provide other critical services. Yet, our GA administrators continue to make every effort to process applications as quickly as possible so our citizens do not go without basic necessities.
Over the years, GA administrators from across the state made the case to the Health and Human Services Committee that they would be more efPicient and effective if they had access to a statewide database. This Committee and the Legislature responded in 2024 by enacting a law requiring the Department of Health and Human Services develop a database and provide municipalities with access to it by July 1, 2025. According to the Department, proposals exceeded the budget and adequate funding has not been available to proceed.

Since the Legislature determined a statewide database was necessary enough to include in statute and given the continuing requests for one, we ask that you vote ought not to pass on LD 1996. Rather than eliminating the potential for developing such essential infrastructure, please consider amending the implementation date to such a time when the database can be adequately funded.
Thank you for your time.

Good morning, Representative Meyer, and fellow colleagues on the Committee on Health and
Human Services. As you know, I am Senator Hemy Ingwersen, and I represent Senate District 32, which includes Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman. Today, I am very pleased to introduce a bill on behalf of the Department, LD 1996, "An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of
the State in the Laws Governing General Assistance."
I have sponsored this bill on behalf of the Office for Family Independence, an office within the
Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), of which we are all familiar. This bill
removes the specific requirement that DHHS provide overseers of each municipality's general
assistance program access to internet-based, real-time data containing the information necessary to properly determine eligibility of an applicant for GA. The bill also updates certain reporting requirements for the Department.
I know that all of us in this room have a shared desire to improve the availability of data and
information regarding the usage of our GA program. It has been a focus of this committee, and I
know that it will continue to be. When the Legislature voted in the first session of the l32nd
Legislattne to approve this specific provision, the separate but accompanying policy that would
have provided the necessary appropriations was not approved. As we've heard from the Department -- and I'm sure they will reiterate this point today -- the establishment of an online
database is simply too costly. The removal of this requirement will ensure the Department is not out of compliance with the statute moving forward.
I hope that you will join me in supporting this bill. The Department will follow my testimony,
and I ask that you hold any questions you may have for the Department.
Thank you.

Testimony of the Office for Family Independence
Maine Department of Health and Human Services
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
In support of LD 1996, An Act to Clarijj/ Responsibilities of the State in the Laws
Governing General Assistance
Sponsor: Senator Ingwersen Hearing Date: January 29, 2026
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health
and Human Services, my name is Ian Yaffe, and I serve as the Director of the Office for Family Independence (OFI) in the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. I am here today to testify in support of LD 1996 An Act to Clarifii Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing
General Assistance.
The Department appreciates the Legislature's intent in establishing a statewide General Assistance
database and enhanced reporting requirements, and we share the goal of improving the availability
of data and information regarding the usage of the GA program. At the time the statutory
requirement for the provision of a statewide database was enacted, the Department believed it could absorb the expense to implement necessary software and did not anticipate the level of cost required to build and maintain a secure, statewide system for a municipally administered program. In August 2024, the Department launched a Request for Proposals (RFP) to build a technology platform for
the GA program. Evaluation of these bids began earlier this year. The bids received ranged between
$752,000 to $5,819,329 for the Initial Period of Performance (2 years). As planning progressed, it became clear that the scope and cost of a statewide General Assistance database exceeded what the Department can responsibly absorb Within current funding. As a result, the Department is now
faced with a statutory requirement that cannot be fully implemented within current resources. Given
the current fiscal reality and ongoing increases to costs within the GA program, the Department
cannot absorb these costs into Department resources as it originally intended.
Based on this financial reality, the Department proposes to:
0 Repeal the requirement for the Department to provide an "Internet-based, real-time database containing the information necessary to properly determine an applicant's
eligibility."
0 Slightly modify the reporting requirements for the Department based on what can be
reported Without the database, using changes to the existing GA reimbursement form which
would be effective on July 1, 2025, enabling a partial report for the January 2026 deadline
for the report.

This bill provides a narrow, technical correction by removing the unfunded database mandate and related reporting requirement, bringing statute back into alignment with what can be operationally and fiscally supported.
The Department also wants to clarify the legislative history of this issue. In the prior legislative session (lst session of the 132""), the Legislature voted to approve this change to address the lack of
a GA data system, however, that provision was coupled with a separate policy change in H.P. 63 8,
L.D. 978 that carried a fiscal impact. As a result, while the policy language advanced, the necessary
appropriations did not pass. This bill, LD 1996, separates this narrow, technical correction from
broader policy considerations, allowing the Legislature to address this issue independently and prevent ongoing statutory noncompliance.
The Department supports this bill and remains committed to transparency and accountability within
the General Assistance program. We respectfully request the Committee's support of this bill as a
standalone measure to prevent continued noncompliance and allow the Department and Legislature to revisit system modernization in the future if funding becomes available.
Thank you for your time and attention, I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

MEJ Testimony opposing LD 1996, An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing General Assistance
January 29, 2026
Good morning, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Health and Human Services Committee. My name is Dina Malual and I am a Policy Advocate with Maine Equal Justice (MEJ), a nonprofit legal aid provider working to increase economic security, opportunity, and equity for people in Maine.
Maine Equal Justice has worked on General Assistance since we were founded in the mid-90s, and some of our staff have worked on it for more than 40 years. In our legal services work, our engagement with low-income Mainers around public policies, and our advocacy work at the State House, with DHHS, and with municipalities, we have seen how General Assistance (GA) is an essential part of our safety net for Mainers in every region of our state, and we also have a great deal of experience with aspects of the program that need to be improved.
For these reasons, we stand in front of this committee and ask that you reject LD 1996. In the 131st Session, with leadership from this committee, the legislature passed LD 1732, which took several steps to improve the GA program, including the creation of a database by DHHS that would better provide data to inform policy decisions. Beginning July 1, 2025, the Department would use information from a real-time, internet-based database to improve GA eligibility and determination.
Despite enactment, the database was never created. In testimony last year on LD 637, Resolve, Directing the Department of Health and Human Services to Evaluate the Municipal General Assistance, which was duplicative statutory requirements passed in LD 1732 the previous session, the Department opposed LD 637 and cited high costs for the database delay. A Request for Proposals (RFP) had been launched to build a technology platform for the GA program and bids for the first year ranged between $670,000 to $3,700,000, increasing the following years, which the Department felt were too costly given other budgetary concerns.
As you know, this committee ultimately decided to amend another bill last year to repeal the database requirement, however that bill died. LD 1996 would repeal the database requirement and remove the requirement for the Department to report on the length of time individuals receive assistance. While this bill aligns with actions this committee took last year, we still ask that you reconsider.

General Assistance is needed now more than ever. At a time where state and federal program eligibility is narrowing and living costs are increasing, the demand for food and shelter is dire. Database and reporting requirements were introduced in 2023 and this year we will finally have more accurate and comprehensive data to support policy decisions, but it will be an incomplete picture of what is happening.
While we understand the cost challenge of creating a new database, we believe a database is vital to ensure effective administration. We also believe maintaining information about the length of time individuals or households receive assistance is important because of recent proposals to limit the period of time people can access assistance. How can we understand the implications of such a change if we don't have data about it?
For these reasons, we ask that the Joint Standing Committee of Health and Human Services delay the database rather than repeal it. Reporting without consistent data will be incomplete. A database can help ensure that we have a full picture about the individuals and families who received GA, the length of time assistance was received, and the types of assistance received.
While cost concerns are real, there are choices legislators can make to ensure we have adequate funding both for the assistance GA provides and for transparent administration of the program, which should include a database.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment. We urge you to reject LD 1996. I am happy to answer any questions and can be available for any work sessions.

10059156:
LD 1996, An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing General Assistance
January 29, 2026
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Paige Kombakis, and I am submitting testimony in opposition to LD 1996 on behalf of the Maine Welfare Directors Association Executive Board.
Implementation of a statewide database remains a critical need for General Assistance administrators around the state. A comprehensive database has the potential to reduce administrative error rates, fraud cases, and could increase data reporting accuracy to the Department.
Maine Welfare Directors Association remains committed to ensuring efficient, standardized, and equitable administration of the General Assistance program throughout the state and a statewide database is one tool that we believe has the potential to assist in that mission.
The Department previously indicated their own interest in implementation of a database. When they were approached earlier this winter with a proposal from a software company working on a pilot database we were hopeful that we would see a resolution to this matter. However, the Department declined the proposal, again, citing budgetary restrictions, despite a proposal that was well below previous bids and already in early development stages.
Investment in a database would mean availability of statewide data that could be used to inform future policy and funding decisions for the General Assistance program. While data driven decision making is becoming commonplace in public policy spaces there is a stark lack of reliable or timely data available for the General Assistance program.
It is for these reasons that the MWDA Executive Board urges the committee to vote Ought Not to Pass on LD 1996. An elimination of the database required by statute would be a disservice to municipalities and administrators throughout the state, our applicants, and tax payers.

MAINE SERVICE CENTERS COALITION

Testimony of the Maine Service Centers Coalition LD 1996, An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing
General Assistance
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, the Maine Service Centers Coalition is submitting testimony in opposition to LD 1996, An Act to Clarify Responsibilities of the State in the Laws Governing General Assistance.
The Maine Service Centers Coalition, comprised of 27 towns and cities across the state, articulates the importance of healthy and thriving service center communities, advocates for public policy that supports and contributes to the economic and social viability of our communities, and collaborates with municipal officials, legislators, state agencies and nonprofits to pursue quality of life for all who live and work in our state.
In the 131st Legislature, Representative Meyer introduced LD 1732, legislation recognizing the growing need for the state's General Assistance program as well as "the demand on the municipal staff who administer the program." The bill, she said, "seeks a solution that both protects the state's most vulnerable and supports the communities that implement the program." One of the bill's proposals "to further support effective administration of the program" would "create a statewide database to track program applicants and expenses so that we can make the best use of our resources."
The Health and Human Service Committee unanimously passed LD 1732 with the provision the Department of Health and Human Services "provide overseers access to an Internet-based, real-time database containing the information necessary to properly determine an applicant's eligibility" for the state's GA program beginning July 1, 2025. The legislation was enacted by both Chambers and became law on March 27, 2024.
Our Coalition highlights Representative Meyer's words as they ring even truer today - the GA program is vital and growing, and pressures on our staffs continue to increase. An accessible database remains a critical, and frequently requested, tool that our cities and towns seek in order to: 1) administer the state's GA program more efficiently and cost-effectively; and 2) alleviate some of the strain placed on our already stretched personnel and finances.
The Maine Service Centers Coalition respectfully urges you to join us in opposing LD 1996 and sustaining the law requiring the development of a statewide database for the General Assistance program.
Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.
